description:
AIAC-IT is a technology and engineering club at the Mohammed VI International Academy of Civil Aviation, Morocco. We bring together passionate students interested in Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Software Development, Web Development, and Cybersecurity.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to collaborate, exchange ideas, and build innovative solutions to real-world challenges using technology and creativity.

Think big, build together, and explore beyond boundaries!
summary: Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive 3D web experience about the machines humanity left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Visitors start in a live 3D Solar System, pick a destination, and ride a spacecraft that launches from Earth to that world. There, every landing site is pinned at its real coordinates, and each of the 20 machines can be visited up close: Apollo landers, rovers such as Opportunity and Sojourner, Viking, InSight, Ingenuity, and probes such as Voyager 1 and Cassini. Each machine has a kid-friendly story with cited sources. It also has an interactive 3D blueprint diagram with labels pinned to its real parts, built from NASA’s own 3D models. The project answers the challenge by turning scattered mission records into one explorable archive. It shows where this equipment still lies, what it discovered and how its mission ended. This matters because these machines are part of our scientific heritage, and most people don’t know they’re still out there.
details:
What it does: The app opens on a 3D Solar System (the Sun, eight planets on their orbits, the asteroid belt, the Moon and a deep-space beacon), with facts on hover. The catalogue has three categories: the Moon, Mars and Deep Space. Choosing a world or a machine launches a spacecraft from Earth; the camera follows it, then lands at the real site. Each world shows a globe with every machine pinned at its true coordinates; nearby sites are spread apart so none hides another. At a machine you get a close-up of its 3D model on procedurally generated terrain, its story, discoveries, mission data and sources. A “3D Diagram” tab shows a rotatable blueprint of the same model with labels on its real parts (antennas, nuclear power units, landing legs, the Golden Record…). There are also sound effects (rocket, Mars wind, Moon hum) and a show/hide text button.

Benefits and impact: It turns NASA mission records into a story that school-age visitors can explore. It teaches where human hardware remains across the Solar System, what each machine achieved, and why preserving this history matters. Every fact cites a source, and each model is labelled honestly as the exact NASA model, a NASA model of an identical twin spacecraft, or an illustrative stand-in.

Tools: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, three.js, React Three Fiber, drei and zustand. Sounds, planet surfaces, terrain and the spacecraft are generated in code, so there are no copyrighted assets.

Creativity: A cinematic flight from Earth to each site, blueprint diagrams pinned to real parts of NASA models, and an “access” animation when a machine’s record opens.

What we considered: Accuracy (sources for every fact, honest model labels, real landing coordinates, a “not to scale” notice), accessibility (keyboard-usable buttons, reduced-motion support, phone layout) and performance (adaptive quality; the 3D diagram pauses the main scene).
